extracted.intended_audience: readers of Renaissance satire and authors/students of satirical/humorous prose
extracted.subtask_description: Producing or analyzing a satirical essay that praises folly and inverts conventional moral/ethical criteria to show the social value of foolishness. Targets rhetorical strategies, comedic devices, and social critique typical of Renaissance humanist satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folly as social seasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Folly 'seasons and sweetens' rough temper; it softens harshness in relationships and makes life pleasant rather than austere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use folly to temper 'the roughness of the masculine temper' and to produce pleasure: show how comic excesses or 'folly' humanize otherwise severe characters. Example language: 'seasoned and sweetened by her folly.' Anti-pattern: portraying constant grim seriousness as desirable without relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of buffoons and jests to entertain social gatherings
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is no natural occasion for laughter, bring in 'one that may make it'—a buffoon or flatterer—to 'put by the gravity of the company.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For scenes of feasting or communal celebration, include hired entertainers, games, and playful rituals (choosing a king, throwing dice, dancing the cushion) because 'there was never any pleasant which folly gave not the relish to.' Anti-pattern: rigidly realistic dinners without comic relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folly as the glue of friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Overlooking or admiring friends' faults—kissing a wart, praising a squint-eyed child—is 'mere folly' but is what 'joins friends together and continues them so joined.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray tolerance, flattering blindness, and small deceptions among friends as virtues that maintain bonds. Use concrete, slightly absurd examples to illustrate how small follies sustain friendship. Avoid moralizing critiques that call such tolerance simply vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrimony sustained by flattery and dissembling
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriage is 'supported and cherished by flattery, apishness, gentleness, ignorance, dissembling' — small follies that prevent divorce and domestic upheaval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In depicting domestic life, emphasize mutual self-deception and performative affection as stabilizing elements. Show how ignorance/neglect on both sides often keeps couples together. Anti-pattern: idealizing marriage as sustained only by truth and perfect reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small social failings maintain social order
rubrics_metrics.description: Society endures because people 'sweeten one another with some small relish of folly'—flattery, connivance, and reciprocal softening make hierarchical relations tolerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining institutions or social hierarchies, highlight petty courtesies and flattering practices as functional rather than merely corrupting. Example list from text: governors, servants, masters, scholars, friends, usurers—none would endure without such failings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-love as necessary precondition for art and social esteem
rubrics_metrics.description: Everyone must 'flatter himself and commend himself to himself' — self-love enables orators, musicians, actors, poets, painters, and physicians to perform and be appreciated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict confidence/self-flattery as enabling creative and social action; show the collapse of public life if performers lacked self-regard. Anti-pattern: portraying self-effacement as always noble or more productive than self-assurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage and bluntness over refined wisdom in enterprises (including war)
rubrics_metrics.description: Great enterprises, including war, are often driven by 'blunt, fat fellows' whose courage surpasses the refined understanding of philosophers; wisdom can be an obstacle to action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast theoretical wisdom with practical daring: valorize actors who act without overthinking. In comedic or satirical scenes, make excessive deliberation a handicap. Example contrast: Demosthenes as orator vs soldiers chosen for courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophers and excessive wisdom are ill-suited for public life
rubrics_metrics.description: Wise men are often 'unfortunate' in public affairs—Socrates, Plato, Cicero cited—and their wisdom can make them ineffective governors or generals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use irony to show the mismatch between philosophical life and popular/governmental needs. Present excessive seriousness or hyper-refinement as socially alienating; dramatize the social value of 'middle sort of fools' who can command and please the many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fables, myths, and simple inventions rule the masses better than philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Political success with the people comes from 'ridiculous and childish fable[s]' and 'fabulous inventions' (e.g., Amphion, Themistocles' tales) rather than philosophical orations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting persuasive popular rhetoric in satire, prefer vivid stories, emblems, and simple myths to abstract argumentation. Examples: the white hind, emblematic tales; anti-pattern: relying on dense philosophical argument to sway a populace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arts and fame spring from folly (thirst of glory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Men undertake arts and painstaking labor driven by 'the thirst of glory'—a kind of folly—from which posterity benefits ('you reap the benefit of other men's madness').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame creative ambition as simultaneously foolish and socially productive: artists' vanity yields works that please others. Use paradox to praise the foolish motives behind admired works of culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence through bold experience (fool's practical wisdom)
rubrics_metrics.description: If prudence is learned by experience, the fool who 'attempts and ventures' acquires true practical prudence that cautious wise men, held back by modesty and fear, lack ('The fool... gathers, if I mistake not, the true prudence').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray trial-and-error, rashness, and embarrassment as sources of real-world knowledge. Favor scenes of active trying over characters paralyzed by overanalysis. Anti-pattern: equating theoretical study with adequate life competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roleplay and disguise as essential entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: Life is 'a kind of comedy' where impersonation—acting as woman/man, king/peasant—entertains; exposing the disguise would spoil the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ theatrical devices, masks, and role reversals in satire/ comedy to produce amusement; protect the illusion—do not 'strip him of his disguise' unless the aim is shock rather than entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions (folly) as incentives to virtue and human feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Passions are not mere vices but 'spurs and incentives' that encourage well-doing; Stoic removal of all affection creates an inhuman 'stony semblance of a man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent emotions and irrational impulses as motivating forces that yield social goods—love, pity, courage—rather than solely as obstacles to reason. Anti-pattern: depicting passionless virtue as unquestionably superior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for natural art and common sense over abstruse learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Arts nearest to 'common sense', those that follow Nature and folly, are happiest and most successful; excessive sciences can be 'pests of mankind' and obstruct happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In satirical critique of learning, valorize crafts and practices rooted in everyday life (physic as practiced, law-drivers) and mock abstruse or scholastic pursuits as disconnected. Use examples like the bee's architecture vs philosophical constructs. Anti-pattern: unqualified praise of specialized learning as always beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folly as preservative of desire to live (counter to misanthropic wisdom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Folly 'sprinkle[s] pleasure with the hopes of good and sweeten[s] men up in their greatest misfortunes' so that people remain attached to life despite misery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing despair or melancholic themes in satire, show small pleasures, self-deceptions, and comic vanities as life-preserving. Example: aged people dyeing hair, marrying young—ridiculed yet preferable to suicide.
